new_statements.quote: Me imagino que poco a poco los nauahablantes adaptaron una parte de la prosodia del español a su propio nauatl, introduciendo la pronunciación con más fuerza en la penúltima sílaba. Esto es lo que encontramos en todos los dialectos del nauatl de hoy, si bien la diferencia entre vocales largas y vocales cortas persiste en casi todos ellos. [p. 93] [...] Sabemos que hoy en día los hablantes de todos los dialectos del nauatl pronuncian sus palabras con más fuerza en la penúltima sílaba. Me imagino que este nuevo rasgo en el nauatl se debe a la influencia del español como lengua dominante. [p. 94]
new_statements.translation: I imagine that little by little the Nahuatl speakers adapted part of Spanish word prosody into their own Nahuatl, introducing the stronger pronunciation of the penultimate syllable. This is what we find in all Nahuatl dialects today, although the difference between long and short vowels persists in almost all of them. [...] We know that nowadays the speakers of all Nahuatl dialects pronounce their words with more force on the penultimate syllable. I imagine that this new trait in Nahuatl is due to the influence of Spanish as the dominant language.
new_statements.citation: Canger, Una. 2018. ¿Por qué los topónimos México y Chapultepec tienen acento en la primera y en la última sílaba? Estudios de Cultura Náhuatl 55: 87-95.
new_statements.locator: pp. 93-94 (section on 20th-century Nahuatl prosody, following the loanword tables)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened (10 PDF pages, text layer present; extracted text, no scanned). Both quoted passages are verbatim: p. 93 (PDF page 7) 'Me imagino que poco a poco los nauahablantes adaptaron una parte de la prosodia del español a su propio nauatl, introduciendo la pronunciación con más fuerza en la penúltima sílaba. Esto es lo que encontramos en todos los dialectos del nauatl de hoy, si bien la diferencia entre vocales largas y vocales cortas persiste en casi todos ellos.' and p. 94 (PDF page 8) 'Sabemos que hoy en día los hablantes de todos los dialectos del nauatl pronuncian sus palabras con más fuerza en la penúltima sílaba. Me imagino que este nuevo rasgo en el nauatl se debe a la influencia…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (prominence) falls on the penultimate syllable in every modern Nahuatl dialect, independent of contrastive vowel length, which is retained (e.g. 16th-c. loans tomi:n, kosta:l are now tómi:n, kósta:l with penult prominence and a long final vowel). Canger treats penult prominence as a post-conquest Spanish-induced innovation; 16th-century Urban Nahuatl is described as having had vowel quantity but no prominent syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: For Coatepec none. The Durango (Mexicanero) dialect is singled out as the one dialect where contrastive vowel length has been lost and stress has become morphologically active like Spanish (taxkál vs no-táxkal; ki-tás vs ki-tasá), citing Canger 2000. The vocative final stress of Classical Nahuatl is quoted from Newman 1967, not asserted for modern dialects.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('sus palabras'); no separate phrase-level or citation-form discussion. The statement is a blanket claim over all present-day Nahuatl dialects by the linguist who did the Coatepec de los Costales fieldwork (Canger 2021 grammar); it does not name Coatepec explicitly, and Coatepec is only implied as one of the 'dialectos del nauatl de hoy'.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is a pan-Nahuatl generalization ('todos los dialectos del nauatl de hoy'), not a statement naming Coatepec Nahuatl (coat1240); it comes from Una Canger, whose fieldwork variety is Coatepec de los Costales and who is the author of the variety's only grammar (2021). Coatepec Nahuatl = Glottolog coat1240 = ISO naz, spoken in Coatepec de los Costales and Chilacachapa, north Guerrero; Canger 2022 calls it 'North Guerrero Nawatl' / 'Coatepec Nawatl' and argues it has a Guerrero Chontal substrate. It is distinct from Guerrero (Balsas) Nahuatl guer1243 [ngu] and from Classical/Urban Nahuatl. The variety-specific description (Canger 2021) and the 1941 phonemic sketch (McQuown) remain unopened.

sources.locator: pp. 93-94 (section on 20th-century Nahuatl prosody, following the loanword tables)
sources.note: Whole article is on Nahuatl word prosody: 16th-c. Urban Nahuatl had no prominent syllable, only vowel length; all present-day Nahuatl dialects pronounce the penultimate syllable with more force (pp. 93-94), a trait she attributes to Spanish influence; vowel length persists in almost all dialects; Durango (Mexicanero) is the only dialect she has found with loss of contrastive length and morphologically active Spanish-like stress. Pan-Nahuatl statement, not Coatepec-specific, but by the author of the only grammar of Coatepec Nahuatl.
